questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-3y=g(x).
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}:$According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Substituting the expressions $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation yields the following relationship between ${u}_{1}^{′},{u}_{2}^{′},$ and $g(x):$

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′}.
$$

Next, we substitute $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-3y & =g(x) \\ ({y}_{p}^{′})^{′}+2{y}_{p}^{′}-3{y}_{p} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Using our expressions for ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′})}^{′}+2({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′})-3({u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}) & =g(x) \\ {({u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}-3{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x} & =g(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}+9{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}-3{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group all terms proportional to ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}{{({e}^{x}+2{e}^{x}-3{e}^{x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{2}{{(9{e}^{-3x}-6{e}^{-3x}-3{e}^{-3x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the expressions in parentheses are both zero. Therefore, the equation reduces to

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=g(x).
$$

questions.problem:

$$

$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-x}.$ 

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}:$

$$
{{field-4}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-x})}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x})}^{′}+{({u}_{2}{e}^{-x})}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} & ={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-x})^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} & =2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}-{u}_{2}{e}^{-x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}-\cancel{{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}} & =\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{{u}_{2}{e}^{-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}=0.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\cancel{{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\cancel{{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\cancel{{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\cancel{{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0.
$$
